name: Big-O and Complexity
author: Recurse
subject: cs
description: Count the work code does and predict how it scales: growth classes, loops, recursion trees, space, amortized cost.

lesson.intro: Big-O is how programmers predict whether code will still be fast when the input gets a thousand times bigger. This pack teaches you to count the work an algorithm does, simplify it into a growth class, analyze loops and recursion, account for memory and amortized costs, and talk about all of it clearly in an interview.
objectives: Count the steps an algorithm takes and simplify the count to Big-O
Classify sequential, nested, halving and recursive code by its growth class
Distinguish best, average, worst and amortized cost, and time from space
State and defend the complexity of your own solution in an interview

sections.title: Counting operations, then dropping the details
sections.body:
Two developers time the same function. One gets 40 ms on a laptop, the other 9 ms on a workstation. Which number describes the algorithm? Neither. Seconds depend on the hardware, the language, whatever else is running and the particular input. To compare algorithms we need something that depends only on the algorithm: how the amount of work **grows** as the input grows.

So we count steps. Pick a basic operation (a comparison, an assignment, an arithmetic step) and count how many times it runs as a function of the input size n. The function `total` below does about n + 2 steps for a list of n numbers. `count_pairs` does about n^2/2, because it visits every pair.

Exact counts are fussy and depend on what you call a step, so **Big-O** keeps only what matters for large n:

- **Drop constant factors.** 2n and 100n are both O(n). Constants depend on the machine and the details; the shape of growth does not.
- **Drop lower-order terms.** n^2 + 1000n + 5 is O(n^2). At n = 1,000,000 the n^2 term is a trillion while 1000n is a billion, a 0.1 percent difference, and the gap keeps widening.

Formally, f(n) is O(g(n)) if f(n) stays below c × g(n) for some constant c once n is large enough. Big-O is an **upper bound**: the work grows no faster than g. It has two relatives: Big-Omega (Ω) is a lower bound, and Big-Theta (Θ) means both at once, a tight bound. In interviews and everyday talk people say Big-O but mean the tight bound, so call a linear scan O(n), not O(n^2), even though the looser claim is technically true.

Dropping constants has a cost worth remembering: Big-O predicts the winner for large inputs, not for every input. An algorithm doing 100n steps loses to one doing n^2 steps until n passes 100. That is why library sorts switch to simple insertion sort for tiny arrays.
sections.pitfall: Keeping constants in the answer. O(2n) and O(n/2) are both written O(n), and O(n^2 + n) is written O(n^2). Interviewers notice when you do not simplify.

check.question: Algorithm A takes 2n steps and algorithm B takes 50n steps. How do their Big-O classes compare?
choices: A is O(n) and B is O(n^2)
Both are O(n): B is about 25 times slower at every size, but both grow the same way
B is O(50n), which is a different class from O(n)
A is faster only for small n
check.explanation: Constant factors are dropped, so both are O(n): doubling n doubles the work of each. The factor of 25 is real and can matter in practice, but it never changes, which is exactly what Big-O sets aside.

sections.title: The common growth classes
sections.body:
Most algorithms you meet fall into a handful of classes. Learn each with one example and you can classify new code by resemblance.

- **O(1), constant**: the work does not depend on n. Indexing an array, pushing onto a stack, a dict lookup on average.
- **O(log n), logarithmic**: each step throws away a constant fraction of what is left. Binary search, a balanced tree lookup, a heap push. Doubling n adds just one step.
- **O(n), linear**: touch each item a constant number of times. Summing a list, finding the maximum, a linear search.
- **O(n log n), linearithmic**: the cost of good sorting (merge sort, Timsort) and many divide and conquer algorithms. Only a little worse than linear in practice.
- **O(n^2), quadratic**: compare every pair, usually with nested loops. Bubble sort, checking all pairs for duplicates.
- **O(2^n), exponential**: try every subset, or recurse twice per call n levels deep. Naive Fibonacci, brute-force subset problems.
- **O(n!), factorial**: try every ordering. Brute-force traveling salesperson.

The table shows why the class matters more than any constant. At n = 1,000,000, an O(n log n) algorithm does about 20 million steps, well under a second on a typical machine (a few hundred million simple steps per second is a fair rough figure, more in compiled languages). An O(n^2) algorithm does a trillion steps, which takes hours, and an O(2^n) one would not finish before the sun burns out.

A handy way to predict running time is to ask what happens when n doubles. O(1) stays the same, O(log n) adds one step, O(n) doubles, O(n log n) slightly more than doubles, O(n^2) quadruples and O(2^n) squares. If a quadratic job takes 2 seconds on 10,000 items, plan for about 8 seconds on 20,000.

activity.title: Watch the curves race
activity.prompt: Drag n from 1 up to 64 and watch the curves separate: for small n they look alike, but by 64, 2^n is off the chart while log n has barely moved. Then rank the classes from slowest growing to fastest growing.

sections.pitfall: Thinking O(log n) is nearly as slow as O(n). log2 of a billion is about 30. A logarithmic algorithm barely notices when its input grows a thousandfold.

check.question: An O(n) job takes 3 seconds on 1 million items. Roughly how long will it take on 4 million?
choices: 48 seconds
3 seconds
12 seconds
6 seconds
check.explanation: Linear work scales with n, so 4 times the input means about 4 times the time: 12 seconds. 48 seconds is what an O(n^2) job would do (4 squared is 16).

sections.title: Analyzing loops: nested, halving and hidden
sections.body:
Most complexity analysis is reading loops. A few rules cover nearly everything:

- **Sequential blocks add.** A loop over n followed by another loop over n is n + n = 2n, which is O(n). Then keep only the biggest term: an O(n^2) block followed by an O(n) block is O(n^2).
- **Nested loops multiply.** An outer loop of n iterations around an inner loop of n iterations is n × n = O(n^2). But check what the inner loop depends on: an inner loop of exactly 10 iterations makes the total 10n, which is O(n).
- **Dependent nested loops still multiply.** If the inner loop runs i times on the i-th outer pass, the total is 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) = n(n - 1)/2, which is O(n^2). Starting the inner loop at i + 1 halves the work but does not change the class.
- **Halving or doubling loops are logarithmic.** A loop that does `i //= 2` until i reaches 1, or `i *= 2` until i reaches n, runs about log2(n) times. Put one inside a loop over n and you get O(n log n).
- **Different inputs get different letters.** A loop over list A nested inside a loop over list B is O(a × b), not O(n^2). Two separate loops over them are O(a + b).

The most common mistake is missing **hidden loops**. A single line can do O(n) work:

- `x in some_list`, `some_list.index(x)`, `some_list.count(x)`, `min`, `max` and `sum` all scan the list.
- Slicing (`nums[1:]`), copying (`list(nums)`), `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` touch every item.
- Building a string with `s += piece` in a loop can copy the whole string each time; collect pieces in a list and `"".join()` them at the end.
- `sorted()` and `.sort()` cost O(n log n).

Put one of those inside a loop over n and you have an O(n^2) function that looks like O(n) at first glance.
sections.code:
def has_common(a, b):            # a has n items, b has m items
    for x in a:                  # n iterations
        if x in b:               # hidden loop: up to m steps if b is a list
            return True
    return False                 # O(n × m) with a list,
                                 # O(n + m) if b is made a set first

def halvings(n):
    steps = 0
    while n > 1:                 # n, n/2, n/4, ..., 1
        n //= 2
        steps += 1
    return steps                 # about log2(n)

print(halvings(1_000_000))       # 19
sections.pitfall: Assuming every nested loop is O(n^2). Check what each loop actually depends on: a constant inner loop keeps the total linear, and a halving inner loop gives O(n log n).

check.question: A loop runs over n items, and on every iteration it calls sorted() on a list of n items. What is the total time complexity?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n^2 log n)
check.explanation: Each sorted() call costs O(n log n), and it runs n times: n × n log n = O(n^2 log n). The fix is usually to sort once, before the loop.

sections.title: Best, average and worst case
sections.body:
Search a list for a name. If the name is first, you are done in one step; if it is last or missing, you check everything. Same algorithm, same n, very different amounts of work. So a complexity claim should say which **case** it describes.

- **Best case**: the friendliest input of size n. Linear search's best case is O(1). Rarely useful on its own, since every algorithm looks good on its best day.
- **Worst case**: the most expensive input of size n. This is what an unqualified Big-O usually means, and the one to use when you need a guarantee: a server endpoint, a real-time system, or input an attacker gets to choose.
- **Average case**: the expected cost over typical or random inputs. It requires an assumption about what inputs look like, but it often matches real-world behavior best.

Famous examples where the cases differ:

- Quicksort: O(n log n) on average, O(n^2) in the worst case (consistently bad pivots).
- Hash table lookup: O(1) on average, O(n) in the worst case when many keys collide.
- Insertion sort: O(n) in the best case (already sorted), O(n^2) on average and in the worst case.
- Binary search: O(1) in the best case (the first middle is the target), O(log n) in the worst.

Do not confuse these cases with Big-O, Omega and Theta. "Worst case" chooses which input you analyze; Big-O versus Theta says how tightly you bound the work on that input. You can give a tight bound for the worst case, and that is what people usually do.
sections.pitfall: Quoting a best case as if it were typical. "Bubble sort is O(n)" is only true for already sorted input with an early exit. Say "O(n^2) on average and in the worst case, O(n) at best".

check.question: Why do engineers usually quote the worst case?
choices: It is the case that happens most often
It is always the easiest one to compute
It is a guarantee: no input of that size can take longer
Big-O can only describe worst cases
check.explanation: A worst-case bound holds for every input, which is what you need for capacity planning and for inputs you do not control. Big-O can describe any case; it is simply attached to the worst case by default.

sections.title: Recursion trees
sections.body:
Loops are easy to count. Recursive functions are harder, because the work hides in calls that make more calls. The tool is a **recursion tree**: draw each call as a node with its recursive calls as children, note the work each call does apart from its children, and add everything up.

Two quantities usually decide the answer: how many calls each call makes (the **branching factor**) and how deep the tree goes.

- **One call, input shrinks by 1** (summing a list, factorial): a chain of n calls doing O(1) each, so O(n).
- **One call, input halves** (recursive binary search): a chain of about log2(n) calls, so O(log n).
- **Two calls, input shrinks by 1** (naive Fibonacci): the tree roughly doubles at every level and is about n levels deep, so O(2^n). In general, b calls per call over d levels gives up to b^d calls.
- **Two calls, input halves, O(n) work to combine** (merge sort): level 0 does n work; level 1 has two halves doing n/2 each, n in total; level 2 has four quarters, n in total; and so on. Every level costs n and there are log2(n) levels, so O(n log n).

The merge sort tree is worth drawing once by hand, because the "n per level times log n levels" picture explains most O(n log n) algorithms.

Memoization reshapes a tree dramatically. Naive Fibonacci's tree is exponential because the same subproblems appear again and again; caching each result collapses it to one computation per distinct n, which is O(n). Whenever a recursion tree repeats subproblems, that is your signal for memoization or dynamic programming.
sections.code:
Merge sort on n = 8: work per level

level 0:             [8]                    8
level 1:         [4]       [4]              4 + 4 = 8
level 2:       [2] [2]   [2] [2]            2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8
level 3:     [1][1][1][1][1][1][1][1]       base cases

log2(8) = 3 levels of merging, each costing n = 8  ->  n log2 n = 24

Naive fib(5): calls per level 1, 2, 4, 6, 2  ->  15 calls in total,
and the count keeps roughly doubling as n grows

activity.title: Double n, compare the counts
activity.prompt: Run bubble sort and merge sort on the same 12 bars and write down both comparison counts. Now drag the size to 24 and run both again. Doubling n should roughly quadruple bubble sort's count (O(n^2)) but only a little more than double merge sort's (O(n log n)).

sections.pitfall: Counting calls and forgetting the work inside each call. Merge sort makes only about 2n calls, but every level of its tree does O(n) merging, and that is where the n log n comes from.

check.question: A recursive function calls itself twice on inputs half the size and does O(1) other work per call. How many calls happen in total?
choices: O(n): the levels hold 1, 2, 4, ..., n calls, which add up to about 2n
O(log n): the input halves each time
O(n log n): it has the same shape as merge sort
O(2^n): every call makes two more
check.explanation: The tree is log2(n) levels deep, and the levels hold 1, 2, 4, ... up to n calls, a geometric series under 2n. Merge sort is O(n log n) only because each of its levels also does O(n) merging work.

sections.title: Space complexity
sections.body:
Your function passes every test, then dies in production with an out-of-memory error on a large file. Time is not the only resource. **Space complexity** measures how much extra memory an algorithm needs as n grows.

Usually we mean **auxiliary space**: memory beyond the input itself. Reading a list while keeping a running total is O(1) auxiliary space; building a new list of n results is O(n).

What costs space:

- New collections: a copy, a result list, a set of seen items, a dict of counts, a DP table. A 2D table of n by m entries is O(n × m).
- Slices and string operations that create new objects.
- **The call stack.** Every recursive call that has not returned holds a frame. Recursion n levels deep uses O(n) space even if it creates no lists; recursion that halves the input, like binary search, uses O(log n).

Space and time often trade against each other. A set of seen values spends O(n) memory to turn an O(n^2) duplicate check into O(n). A cache spends memory to avoid recomputing. Memoized Fibonacci uses O(n) space to save exponential time. Sometimes the trade runs the other way: sorting in place uses little extra space but destroys the original order.

An **in-place** algorithm modifies its input using O(1) extra space, such as reversing a list by swapping from both ends. In an interview, say whether your solution modifies the input; some interviewers allow it and some do not.
sections.code:
def reverse_copy(nums):          # O(n) extra: a new list of n items
    return nums[::-1]

def reverse_in_place(nums):      # O(1) extra: just two indexes
    i, j = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while i < j:
        nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        i += 1
        j -= 1

def depth(n):                    # O(n) extra: n frames on the call stack
    return 0 if n == 0 else 1 + depth(n - 1)

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
reverse_in_place(nums)
print(nums, reverse_copy(nums), depth(500))   # [4, 3, 2, 1] [1, 2, 3, 4] 500
sections.pitfall: Calling a recursive function O(1) space because it creates no lists. Each pending call is a stack frame, so depth n means O(n) space, and in Python deep enough recursion raises RecursionError.

check.question: Memoized fib(n) stores each result in a dict and recurses up to n levels deep. What is its space complexity?
choices: O(log n)
O(n): up to n cached values plus up to n stack frames
check.explanation: The cache holds one entry per value from 0 to n, and the first descent reaches about n frames deep. Both are O(n), so the total is O(n). O(2^n) describes the time of the naive version, not the space of this one.

sections.title: Amortized analysis
sections.body:
Most appends to a Python list are instant, but every so often one append copies the entire list into a bigger block. So is append O(1) or O(n)? Each answer misses half the story. **Amortized analysis** takes the total cost of a long sequence of operations and divides it by the number of operations.

For a dynamic array that doubles its capacity when full, n appends trigger copies of 1, 2, 4, 8, ... items, up to n. That geometric series sums to less than 2n. Add the n ordinary writes and the total is under 3n, so the **amortized** cost per append is O(1), even though one particular append can cost O(n).

The growth factor is what makes this work. Grow by a fixed 10 slots instead, and a copy happens every 10 appends, copying 10, 20, 30, ... items: about n^2/20 in total, which is O(n) amortized per append. Any constant factor greater than 1 keeps appends O(1) amortized; CPython uses about 1.125, Java's ArrayList 1.5, and many others 2.

Amortized is not the same as average case. Average case is about random inputs; an amortized bound is a guarantee for every sequence of operations, with no luck involved. The idea shows up elsewhere too: hash tables resize like dynamic arrays, so their inserts are O(1) amortized, and a queue built from two stacks dequeues in O(1) amortized.

The catch: an amortized bound says nothing about any single operation. If every operation must be fast, as in a game's frame loop or a low-latency trading system, the occasional O(n) spike can still hurt.

activity.title: Doubling vs adding 10
activity.prompt: Run the simulation, then change n to 20_000 and run it again. Before you do, predict which total will roughly double and which will roughly quadruple, and connect each to O(1) and O(n) amortized appends.

props.code:
def total_copies(n, grow):
    capacity, size, copies = 1, 0, 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if size == capacity:
            copies += size          # move every item to the new block
            capacity = grow(capacity)
        size += 1
    return copies

n = 10_000
print("doubling:", total_copies(n, lambda c: c * 2))
print("plus 10:", total_copies(n, lambda c: c + 10))
props.task: Change n to 20_000 and run it again. Which total doubled and which quadrupled?

sections.pitfall: Saying "append is O(1)" without the word amortized when it matters. A single append can take O(n). If every operation must be fast, preallocate (for example `[0] * n`) or choose a structure without resize spikes.

check.question: A dynamic array grows by adding 100 slots whenever it fills up. What is the amortized cost of an append?
choices: O(1), because 100 is a constant
O(n), because a full copy happens every 100 appends and copies grow with n
O(log n), because the array grows a little each time
O(100), because that is the resize step
check.explanation: Copies of 100, 200, 300, ... items add up to about n^2/200 over n appends, which is O(n) per append on average. Only growth by a constant factor makes the total copying O(n) and each append O(1) amortized.

sections.title: Talking about complexity in interviews
sections.body:
You finish a correct solution and the interviewer asks: "What's the complexity, and can you do better?" This moment is predictable, so prepare for it.

State complexity as one full sentence with four parts:

- **Time and space**, both of them.
- **What the variables mean**: "n is the number of words, m is the length of the longest word".
- **Which case**, when it matters: worst, average or amortized.
- **Where it comes from**: point to the part of the code that dominates.

For example: "Sorting dominates at O(n log n) time; the scan after it is O(n). Extra space is O(n) for the dict."

When asked to do better, find the bottleneck and reach for the classic upgrades:

- Searching inside a loop (O(n^2) overall): a hash set or map makes each lookup O(1).
- Scanning sorted data: binary search or two pointers.
- Recomputing the same subproblems: memoization or a DP table.
- Re-sorting or rescanning to find the minimum again and again: a heap.
- Comparing all pairs: sort first, then sweep once.

Know the **best conceivable runtime** too. If you must read all n inputs, you cannot beat O(n); if the output has n^2 items, you cannot beat O(n^2). Saying "any solution must look at every element at least once, so O(n) is optimal here" shows you know when to stop optimizing.

Constraints in the problem statement hint at the target. With n up to 10^5, O(n^2) means about 10^10 steps, far too slow, so O(n log n) or better is expected. With n up to 20, O(2^n) is fine. With n up to 10^9, think O(log n) or a formula.
sections.pitfall: Giving only a time bound, or a bound with undefined variables. "It's O(n)" invites "what is n?" and "what about space?". Answer both before you are asked.

check.question: A problem says n can be up to 100,000. Which complexity should your solution aim for?
choices: O(n^2), since 100,000 is a small number
O(2^n), since brute force is always acceptable at first
O(n log n) or better, since O(n^2) would be about 10^10 steps
Any complexity: constraints do not hint at the target
check.explanation: 10^10 simple steps take far too long for an interview judge or a web request, while n log n is under 2 million. Reading constraints this way tells you which approach the interviewer expects.

keyTerms.definition: An upper bound on how an algorithm's work grows with input size n, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
A tight bound: the work grows at exactly this rate, up to constant factors. What people usually mean when they say Big-O.
How the number of basic steps grows as the input size grows.
Extra memory an algorithm uses beyond its input, including the call stack.
The cost on the most expensive input of size n. The default meaning of an unqualified Big-O and a guarantee for every input.
The expected cost over typical or random inputs of size n.
Total cost of a sequence of operations divided by their number, so rare expensive steps are spread over many cheap ones.
O(log n): each step discards a constant fraction of the input, so doubling n adds only one step.
A drawing of every recursive call and the work it does, summed level by level to find the total cost.
A single line, such as x in list, a slice or sorted(), that does O(n) or more work behind the scenes.

summary: Big-O describes how work grows with input size: count steps, then drop constants and lower-order terms.
Know the ladder O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n), O(n!) and what doubling n does to each.
Sequential code adds, nested loops multiply, halving loops are logarithmic, and library calls can hide loops.
Say which case you mean: worst case is the default guarantee, average case assumes typical input, and amortized cost spreads rare expensive steps over a sequence.
Recursion trees give recursive costs: branching factor and depth for call counts, work per level times the number of levels for merge-sort-style algorithms.
Space counts too, including the call stack; in interviews state time and space, define n, and name the dominant step.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why one algorithm that takes 1 second on 1,000 items might take 1,000,000 seconds on a million items, while another would take only about 2,000 seconds, and what Big-O has to do with it.

questions.question: What is the simplified Big-O of 3n^3 + 1000n^2 + n?
questions.explanation: Keep only the fastest-growing term and drop its constant. 1000n^2 looks big, but for any n above 333 the 3n^3 term is larger, and the gap keeps widening.

questions.question: Algorithm A takes 100n steps and algorithm B takes n^2 steps. Which statement is true?
choices: A is always faster, because O(n) beats O(n^2)
B is faster for n below 100; A is faster for n above 100
B is always faster, because 100 is a large constant
They are equally fast, because Big-O ignores constants
questions.explanation: n^2 is less than 100n exactly when n is less than 100, so B wins on small inputs. Past n = 100, A pulls ahead and the gap keeps growing. Big-O predicts the winner for large n, not for every n.

questions.question: What does Big-O notation describe?
choices: How an algorithm's work grows as the input size grows
The exact running time of a program in seconds
The number of lines of code in an algorithm
The fastest possible time on the best hardware
questions.explanation: Big-O is about the shape of growth. Seconds depend on the hardware and the language, so Big-O deliberately leaves them out.

questions.question: Which of these operations is O(log n)?
choices: Finding the maximum of an unsorted list
Looking up a key in a dict
Binary search on a sorted list
Sorting a list with sorted()
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the remaining range each step, so it needs about log2(n) steps. Finding a maximum must look at every item, O(n); a dict lookup is O(1) on average; sorting is O(n log n).

questions.question: Naive recursive Fibonacci, where fib(n) calls fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2), is usually given which Big-O time complexity?
questions.explanation: Each call makes two more calls, so the call tree roughly doubles at each level and is about n levels deep. The tight bound is about O(1.62^n), but O(2^n) is the standard answer. Memoization brings it down to O(n).

questions.question: An O(n^2) algorithm takes 2 seconds on 10,000 items. Roughly how long will it take on 20,000 items?
choices: 2 seconds
4 seconds
16 seconds
8 seconds
questions.explanation: Doubling n multiplies n^2 by 4, so 2 seconds becomes about 8. 4 seconds is what an O(n) algorithm would take.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of f for a list of n items?
choices: O(n)
O(2n)
questions.explanation: The nested loops do n * n work and the second loop adds n, giving n^2 + n. Dropping the lower-order term leaves O(n^2). O(2n) would describe two loops one after another, not nested ones.

questions.question: Fill the blank so this loop runs O(log n) times for n >= 1.
questions.code:
count = 0
i = n
while i > 1:
    _____
    count += 1
questions.explanation: Halving i each pass reaches 1 after about log2(n) passes. Subtracting 1 or 2 takes about n or n/2 passes, which are both O(n), and i += 1 never ends.

questions.question: This removes duplicates but is far slower than expected on large lists. What is the problem?
choices: result.append(item) copies the whole list each time
item not in result scans the list every time, making the loop O(n^2); a set would fix it
The for loop visits every item twice
Returning a list is slow; it should return a tuple
questions.explanation: Each `in` check on a list is O(n), and it runs n times, so the total is O(n^2). Keeping a seen set alongside makes each check O(1) on average and the function O(n). append is amortized O(1); it does not copy the list.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of this code?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: The inner loop always runs 10 times, whatever n is, so the total is 10n steps, which is O(n). Nested loops are only O(n^2) when both loops grow with n.

questions.question: Quicksort is often called an O(n log n) sort. Which case does that describe?
choices: Its average case; its worst case is O(n^2)
Its worst case; it is never slower
Its best case; its average case is O(n^2)
Its space complexity, not its time
questions.explanation: With reasonable pivots quicksort splits the list roughly in half each time, giving O(n log n) on average. Consistently bad pivots make it O(n^2), which is why a single Big-O should say which case it means.

questions.question: What is the extra (auxiliary) space complexity of this function? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.code:
def running_totals(nums):
    totals = []
    current = 0
    for x in nums:
        current += x
        totals.append(current)
    return totals
questions.explanation: It builds a new list holding one total per input item, so the extra memory grows with n. The current variable on its own would be O(1).

questions.question: What is the space complexity of this function for a list of n items?
choices: O(1), because it creates no new lists
O(log n), because each call does little work
O(n), because n calls wait on the call stack at once
O(n^2), because each call copies the list
questions.explanation: Before any call returns, the recursion goes n levels deep, and each level keeps a stack frame. No lists are copied here (the index moves instead of slicing), but the stack frames alone cost O(n).

questions.question: Fill the blank so the duplicate check runs in O(n) time.
choices: set()
questions.explanation: A set gives O(1) average membership tests, so the loop is O(n). {} creates an empty dict, not a set, and has no add method. A list has no add method either, and even with append each `in` check would be O(n).

questions.question: Which operation is O(n) on a Python list but O(1) on average on a set?
choices: Adding an item
Checking x in collection
Getting the size with len()
Looping over every item
questions.explanation: A list must compare x with its items one by one; a set jumps to the slot given by x's hash. Adding is O(1) for both (amortized for list append), len is O(1) for both, and looping over everything is O(n) for both.

questions.question: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever it is full. What is the amortized time complexity of one append? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Full copies happen only at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on, and those copies add up to less than 2n over n appends. Shared across the n appends, that is a constant amount each, even though a single resizing append is O(n).

questions.question: Why does a dynamic array grow by a constant factor (such as doubling) instead of adding a fixed 10 slots each time it fills up?
questions.answer: With a fixed increment, a resize happens every 10 appends and each one copies the whole array, so n appends cost O(n^2) in total. Growing by a factor makes resizes rarer as the array grows, so total copying stays O(n) and each append is O(1) amortized.
questions.explanation: The fixed-increment copies are 10 + 20 + 30 + ... + n, about n^2/20 items, which is quadratic. The doubling copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n, which is under 2n.

questions.question: Simplify O(5n + 3n log n + 20).
questions.explanation: n log n grows faster than n, and both outgrow the constant 20. Keep the dominant term and drop its constant factor: O(n log n).

questions.question: An algorithm always takes exactly 3n + 2 steps. Which statement is true?
choices: It is O(n), and also technically O(n^2), because Big-O is only an upper bound
It is O(n) but cannot be called O(n^2)
It is O(3n + 2), and simplifying that would be wrong
It is O(1), because 3 and 2 are constants
questions.explanation: Big-O promises the work grows no faster than the bound, so a looser bound like O(n^2) is still true. The tight bound is Θ(n), and that is what people mean when they say O(n) in practice. Give the tight one in interviews.

questions.question: Match each growth class with a typical example.

pairs.right: Binary search in a sorted list
Finding the maximum of an unsorted list
Listing every subset of a set

questions.explanation: Each class has a signature move: direct access, halving, one pass, divide and conquer with linear combining, all pairs, and all subsets. Recognizing the move is usually enough to classify new code.

questions.question: Order these growth classes from slowest growing to fastest growing.
questions.explanation: For large n each class dwarfs the one before it. Note that n! eventually outgrows 2^n: every extra item multiplies n! by a bigger and bigger number, but 2^n only by 2.

questions.question: With n = 6, what is the value of count after this code runs?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 times, which adds up to 15 = n(n - 1)/2. That is still O(n^2): starting the inner loop at i + 1 halves the work but does not change the growth class.

questions.question: users has n items and products has m items. What is the time complexity?
choices: O(n + m)
O(n × m)
O(max(n, m))
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs m times for each of the n outer iterations, so the work is n × m. Writing O(n^2) assumes both lists have the same size; O(n + m) would describe two separate loops, one after the other.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of this code?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs n, then n/2, then n/4 times, and so on. That geometric series adds up to less than 2n, so the total is O(n). O(n log n) would be right only if the inner loop ran n times on every pass.

questions.question: What is the best-case time complexity of linear search on a list of n items?
choices: O(log n)
O(n): every item is always checked
O(1): the target is the first item
questions.explanation: If the first item matches, linear search stops after one comparison. The worst case, a target that is last or missing, checks all n items, and that is the bound people usually quote.

questions.question: Which statements about hash table lookups are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The average case is O(1)
The worst case is O(n), when many keys land in the same bucket
Resizing makes the worst case O(1)
The best case is O(log n)
questions.explanation: With a good hash function and a sensible load factor, lookups check one short bucket: O(1) on average. If many keys collide, one bucket holds most of them and a lookup degrades to O(n). Resizing keeps the average low but cannot stop deliberate or unlucky collisions.

questions.question: A recursive function makes 3 recursive calls each time, the recursion goes n levels deep, and each call does O(1) other work. What is its time complexity?
questions.explanation: The number of calls triples at every level: 1, 3, 9, 27, ... up to 3^n at depth n. A branching factor of b over depth d gives up to b^d calls, so this is O(3^n).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of this function for a list of n items?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: The slices copy items, so every level of the recursion tree does O(n) copying in total, and there are about log2(n) levels: O(n log n). Passing start and end indexes instead of slicing would make each call O(1) and the whole function O(n).

questions.question: Which of these uses only O(1) extra space?
choices: Building a reversed copy with nums[::-1]
Reversing a list in place by swapping items from both ends
A recursive function that goes n levels deep
Storing every value seen so far in a set
questions.explanation: Swapping from both ends needs only two index variables, however long the list is. The slice builds a whole new list, the recursion holds n stack frames, and the set can grow to n items: all O(n).

questions.question: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. What are the cost of the single worst append and the amortized cost per append?
choices: Worst O(1), amortized O(1)
Worst O(n), amortized O(n)
Worst O(log n), amortized O(1)
Worst O(n), amortized O(1)
questions.explanation: The append that triggers a resize copies all n items, so it is O(n). Those copies happen so rarely (at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ...) that the total over n appends is under 3n, which is O(1) per append amortized.

questions.question: In an interview, what should a complete statement of your solution's complexity include?
questions.answer: Both time and space, what each variable means (for example n is the number of words), which case it is when that matters (worst, average or amortized), and which part of the code dominates the cost.
questions.explanation: For example: 'O(n log n) time, dominated by the sort; O(n) extra space for the dict; n is the number of intervals.' That one sentence answers the interviewer's next three questions before they ask them.

questions.question: Your solution checks every pair of numbers to see if two of them add up to a target: O(n^2). The interviewer asks for something faster. What is the usual next step?
choices: Keep a hash set of numbers seen so far and look up target - x for each x: O(n) time
Sort the list with bubble sort first
Keep the nested loops but stop as soon as a pair is found
Rewrite the loops as recursion
questions.explanation: The inner loop is a search, and a hash set turns each search into an O(1) average lookup, giving O(n) time for O(n) space. Stopping early helps only the best case, and bubble sort is itself O(n^2).

questions.question: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles each time it is full, resizing when it holds 1, 2, 4 and 8 items. How many items are copied in total by those four resizes?
questions.explanation: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 copies by the time the 9th item goes in, under 2 × 9 = 18. Each copy is the size of the array at that moment, and that geometric series always stays below 2n: the heart of the O(1) amortized append.
